subject: maths
title: Sharing and Grouping
seo_title: Year 1 Sharing and Grouping Worksheets: Equal Shares and Equal Groups (Free, Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving equal sharing and grouping; represent the situations with diagrams, physical and virtual materials, and use calculation strategies to solve the problem
meta_desc: Free Year 1 maths worksheets on sharing and grouping: share equally between 2, 3 and 4, spot equal and unequal shares, make groups of 2, 5 and 10, count groups to find the total, and solve simple stories. 100 picture questions with an answer key, following the Australian Curriculum.
key_big: Sharing equally means everyone gets the same. Grouping means the same number in every group.
key_sub: Give out one at a time until none are left. To find the total, count by 2s, 5s or 10s, saying one number for each group.
body_html:
Sharing equally

Sharing equally means everyone gets the same number. Give one to each person. Then give one each again. Keep going until none are left.

Example

Share 12 grapes equally between 3 children.

Give one each, again and again. Each child gets 4. Check: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.

Answer: 4 grapes each

Equal or not equal?

Look at every plate. If they all have the same number, it is equal. If one plate has more, it is not equal. It is not fair.

Making groups

Grouping means putting the same number in each group. Circle 2, 5 or 10 at a time. Then count the groups.

Count the groups to find the total

Say one number for each group. Count by 2s, 5s or 10s.

Example

There are 3 bags. Each bag has 10 marbles. How many marbles?

Count by 10s, one number for each bag: 10, 20, 30.

Answer: 30 marbles

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Unequal shares: 10 grapes as 6 and 4Everyone gets the same: 5 and 5
Counting the groups, not the things: 3 groups of 5 = 3Count every object: 5, 10, 15
Mixing up “groups of 2” and “2 groups”Groups of 2 means 2 in every group
Forgetting yourself: share 8 with 3 friends as 3 childrenYou and 3 friends are 4 children

faq.a: Not with the ÷ sign yet. In the Australian Curriculum (AC9M1N06), Year 1 students solve practical problems by sharing equally and making equal groups, using objects and drawings. This is the start of division and multiplication.

faq.q: What is the difference between sharing and grouping?
faq.a: In sharing, you know how many people and find how many each gets (12 shared between 3 is 4 each). In grouping, you know how many go in each group and find how many groups (12 in groups of 3 is 4 groups).

faq.q: How can I practise sharing and grouping at home?
faq.a: Share real things fairly, like grapes, pegs or Lego bricks, between family members, one at a time. Then put socks in pairs or coins in groups of 5 and 10, and count the groups.

faq.q: Why does my child count the groups instead of the objects?
faq.a: It is a very common Year 1 mistake. Ask “How many in each group?” first, then skip count by that number, saying one number for each group.

items.q: Make the 2 plates equal. How many grapes must move?
items.e: 8 shared between 2 is 4 each. Move 1 grape from the 5 to the 3. Now both have 4. (Moving 2 makes 3 and 5.)
10 shared between 2 is 5 each. Move 1 strawberry from the 6 to the 4. Now both have 5. (Moving 2 makes 4 and 6.)

items.q: Make the 2 plates equal. How many apples must move?

items.q: Make the 2 plates equal. How many biscuits must move?
items.e: 8 shared between 2 is 4 each. Move 3 biscuits from the 7 to the 1. Now both have 4. (Moving 6 makes 1 and 7.)

items.q: Charlotte and Oliver share 10 grapes. Charlotte gets 6. Oliver gets 4. Is it fair?
items.e: 6 and 4 are not the same. Charlotte has more. It is not fair. Fair is 5 each.
3 people get 3 each: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. Everyone has the same, so it is fair.

sets.title: Count the groups to find the total

items.q: How many apples are there altogether?
items.e: Say one number for each group. Count by 2s: 2, 4, 6. There are 6 apples. (3 is the number of groups, not the apples.)

items.q: How many shells are there altogether?
items.e: Say one number for each group. Count by 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8. There are 8 shells. (4 is the number of groups, not the shells.)
Say one number for each group. Count by 5s: 5, 10. There are 10 stickers. (2 is the number of groups, not the stickers.)

Say one number for each group. Count by 5s: 5, 10, 15. There are 15 strawberries. (3 is the number of groups, not the strawberries.)

items.q: Grace has 12 grapes at recess. She shares them equally with Ava. How many does each child get?
items.e: 2 children share 12. Give one each, again and again. Each gets 6. Check: 6 + 6 = 12.

items.e: 10 shared between 2 children is 5 each. Check: 5 + 5 = 10.

items.q: At the sausage sizzle, 3 friends share 6 sausages equally. How many sausages each?
items.e: Give one each: that uses 3. Give one each again: that uses 6. Each friend gets 2. Check: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

items.q: At footy, 4 players share 16 orange slices equally. How many slices each?
items.e: Give one slice to each player, again and again, until none are left. Each player gets 4. Check: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16.

items.q: There are 3 bags. Each bag has 5 apples. How many apples altogether?
items.e: Count by 5s, one number for each bag: 5, 10, 15. There are 15 apples.

items.q: At the class party there are 4 plates. Each plate has 3 biscuits. How many biscuits altogether?
items.e: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 biscuits. (4 is the number of plates.)
Count by 5s to 15: 5, 10, 15. That is 3 fives, so 3 bags.
Count by 5s to 20: 5, 10, 15, 20. That is 4 fives, so 4 students.

items.q: There are 14 children. They sit 2 at each table. How many tables do they need?
items.e: Count by 2s to 14: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. That is 7 twos, so 7 tables.

items.q: 20 students make teams of 5 for sport. How many teams are there?
items.e: Count by 5s to 20: 5, 10, 15, 20. That is 4 teams of 5.
Count by 10s to 30: 10, 20, 30. That is 3 groups of 10.

items.q: 6 children each get 2 orange slices. How many slices is that?
items.e: Count by 2s, one number for each child: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. That is 12 slices.
Count by 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20. There are 20 lollies. (4 + 5 = 9 adds the bags to the lollies.)

items.q: Aarav shares 9 biscuits equally between 3 friends. How many does each friend get?
items.e: Give one each, again and again. Each friend gets 3. Check: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.
Count by 10s: 10, 20. There are 20 strawberries.

items.q: At lunch, Jack shares 20 grapes equally between 4 friends. How many grapes each?
items.e: Give one each, again and again, until none are left. Each friend gets 5. Check: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20.
10 shared between 2 is 5 each. Move 1 from the 6 to the 4. Now 5 and 5. (Moving 2 makes 4 and 6.)

items.q: Zara has 3 bags of 5 marbles. She says, “I have 3 marbles.” How many marbles does she really have?
items.e: 3 is the number of bags. Count the marbles by 5s: 5, 10, 15. Zara has 15 marbles.

items.q: 18 students work in pairs. A pair is 2 students. How many pairs are there?
items.e: Count by 2s to 18: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. That is 9 pairs.

items.q: Leo shares 8 lollies equally with 3 friends. How many lollies does each child get?
items.e: Leo and 3 friends make 4 children. 8 shared between 4 is 2 each. Check: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. (4 each is sharing between only 2.)
